references.label: RCUK PRC 2025
references.citation: Resuscitation Council UK. 2025 Resuscitation Guidelines: Post-resuscitation care guidelines. RCUK; 2025 (algorithm updated March 2026).
references.excerpt: Actively prevent fever by targeting a temperature ≤ 37.5 °C for patients who remain comatose after ROSC from cardiac arrest.

references.label: SCCM PICS 2012
references.citation: Needham DM, Davidson J, Cohen H, et al. Improving long-term outcomes after discharge from intensive care unit: report from a stakeholders' conference. Crit Care Med. 2012;40(2):502-509.
references.excerpt: Postintensive care syndrome was agreed upon as the recommended term to describe new or worsening problems in physical, cognitive, or mental health status arising after a critical illness and persisting beyond acute care hospitalization. The term could be applied to either a survivor or family member.

references.label: BRAIN-ICU 2013
references.citation: Pandharipande PP, Girard TD, Jackson JC, et al. Long-term cognitive impairment after critical illness. N Engl J Med. 2013;369(14):1306-1316.
references.excerpt: At 3 months, 40% of the patients had global cognition scores that were 1.5 SD below the population means (similar to scores for patients with moderate traumatic brain injury), and 26% had scores 2 SD below the population means (similar to scores for patients with mild Alzheimer's disease). Deficits occurred in both older and younger patients and persisted ... A longer duration of delirium was independently associated with worse global cognition at 3 and 12 months

references.label: BRAIN-ICU 2013 sedatives
references.citation: Pandharipande PP, Girard TD, Jackson JC, et al. Long-term cognitive impairment after critical illness. N Engl J Med. 2013;369(14):1306-1316.
references.excerpt: Of the 821 patients enrolled, 6% had cognitive impairment at baseline, and delirium developed in 74% during the hospital stay. ... Use of sedative or analgesic medications was not consistently associated with cognitive impairment at 3 and 12 months.

references.label: Herridge 2011
references.citation: Herridge MS, Tansey CM, Matté A, et al. Functional disability 5 years after acute respiratory distress syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2011;364(14):1293-1304.
references.excerpt: At 5 years, the median 6-minute walk distance was 436 m (76% of predicted distance) ... younger patients had a greater rate of recovery than older patients, but neither group returned to normal predicted levels of physical function at 5 years. Pulmonary function was normal to near-normal. A constellation of other physical and psychological problems developed or persisted in patients and family caregivers for up to 5 years.

references.label: Hatch 2018
references.citation: Hatch R, Young D, Barber V, et al. Anxiety, depression and post traumatic stress disorder after critical illness: a UK-wide prospective cohort study. Crit Care. 2018;22(1):310.
references.excerpt: Postal questionnaires were sent to 13,155 survivors; of these 38% (4943/13155) responded and 55% (2731/4943) of respondents passed thresholds for one or more condition at 3 or 12 months following discharge. Caseness prevalence was 46%, 40% and 22% for anxiety, depression and PTSD respectively ... Patients with symptoms of depression were 47% more likely to die during the first 2 years after discharge from ICU than those without (HR 1.47, CI 1.19-1.80).

references.label: ICU Liberation 2019
references.citation: Pun BT, Balas MC, Barnes-Daly MA, et al. Caring for critically ill patients with the ABCDEF bundle: results of the ICU Liberation Collaborative in over 15,000 adults. Crit Care Med. 2019;47(1):3-14.
references.excerpt: Complete ABCDEF bundle performance was associated with lower likelihood of seven outcomes: hospital death within 7 days (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.32; CI, 0.17-0.62), next-day mechanical ventilation (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 0.28; CI, 0.22-0.36), coma (AOR, 0.35; CI, 0.22-0.56), delirium (AOR, 0.60; CI, 0.49-0.72), physical restraint use (AOR, 0.37; CI, 0.30-0.46), ICU readmission (AOR, 0.54; CI, 0.37-0.79), and discharge to a facility other than home (AOR, 0.64; CI, 0.51-0.80).

references.label: Jones 2010 (ICU diaries)
references.citation: Jones C, Bäckman C, Capuzzo M, et al. Intensive care diaries reduce new onset post traumatic stress disorder following critical illness: a randomised, controlled trial. Crit Care. 2010;14(5):R168.
references.excerpt: Intensive care patients with an ICU stay of more than 72 hours were recruited ... The intervention patients received their ICU diary at 1 month following critical care discharge and the final assessment of the development of acute PTSD was made at 3 months. RESULTS: 352 patients were randomised to the study at 1 month. The incidence of new cases of PTSD was reduced in the intervention group compared to the control patients (5% versus 13%, P = 0.02).

references.label: PRaCTICaL 2009
references.citation: Cuthbertson BH, Rattray J, Campbell MK, et al. The PRaCTICaL study of nurse led, intensive care follow-up programmes for improving long term outcomes from critical illness: a pragmatic randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2009;339:b3723.
references.excerpt: A nurse led intensive care follow-up programme showed no evidence of being effective or cost effective in improving patients' quality of life in the year after discharge from intensive care. Further work should focus on the roles of early physical rehabilitation, delirium, cognitive dysfunction, and relatives in recovery from critical illness.

references.label: NICE CG83 recs
references.citation: NICE. Rehabilitation after critical illness in adults (CG83). 2009, reviewed 2018. Recommendations 1.2-1.3 and 1.23.
references.excerpt: During the patient's critical care stay and as early as clinically possible, perform a short clinical assessment to determine the patient's risk of developing physical and non-physical morbidity ... For patients at risk of physical and non-physical morbidity, perform a comprehensive clinical assessment to identify their current rehabilitation needs. ... Review patients with rehabilitation needs 2 to 3 months after their discharge from critical care.

references.label: NICE NG31
references.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Care of dying adults in the last days of life. NICE guideline NG31. 2015.
references.excerpt: When considering medicines for symptom control, prescribe anticipatory medicines for pain, breathlessness, nausea and vomiting, anxiety or agitation, and noisy respiratory secretions, specifying the starting dose, the minimum interval between doses and the maximum dose in 24 hours, and titrate according to response.

references.label: AoMRC DNC 2008
references.citation: Academy of Medical Royal Colleges. A Code of Practice for the Diagnosis and Confirmation of Death. AoMRC; 2008. Two-stage process: preconditions then clinical tests performed by at least two medical practitioners.

references.label: NHSBT Deceased Donation
references.citation: NHS Blood and Transplant / Organ Donation and Transplantation. Deceased donation pathways: donation after brainstem death (DBD) and donation after circulatory death (DCD), including the 5-minute stand-off after asystole and the role of the specialist nurse for organ donation.

references.label: ERC/ESICM 2021
references.citation: Nolan JP, Sandroni C, Böttiger BW, et al. European Resuscitation Council and European Society of Intensive Care Medicine guidelines 2021: post-resuscitation care. Resuscitation. 2021;161:220-269.
references.excerpt: In patients who are comatose (M ≤ 3) at ≥72 h after ROSC, poor neurological outcome is likely when ≥2 of the following are present: no pupillary and corneal reflexes at ≥72 h; bilaterally absent N20 SSEP wave at ≥24 h; highly malignant EEG at >24 h; NSE >60 μg/L at 48 h and/or 72 h; status myoclonus ≤72 h; or diffuse and extensive anoxic injury on brain CT/MRI. A multimodal approach is mandatory.

references.label: TTM2 2021
references.citation: Dankiewicz J, Cronberg T, Lilja G, et al. Hypothermia versus Normothermia after Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (TTM2). N Engl J Med. 2021;384:2283-2294. Targeted hypothermia at 33°C did not lower 6-month mortality vs. targeted normothermia with early fever treatment (≤37.7°C).

references.label: ILCOR CoSTR 2022
references.citation: Wyckoff MH, Greif R, Morley PT, et al. 2022 International Consensus on CPR and ECC Science With Treatment Recommendations: Executive Summary. Resuscitation. 2022;181:208-288. Recommends active prevention of fever (core temperature ≤37.7°C) for adults post-ROSC; routine cooling to 32–34°C is no longer mandated.

references.citation: General Medical Council. Treatment and care towards the end of life: good practice in decision making. GMC; 2022.

references.citation: UK Parliament. Mental Capacity Act 2005. London: TSO; 2005.

references.citation: NICE. Rehabilitation after critical illness in adults (CG83). 2009.

references.label: RCUK PRC Algorithm March 2026
references.citation: Resuscitation Council UK. Adult post-resuscitation care algorithm, Guidelines 2025, updated March 2026.

cards.question: What ethical framework underpins withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment?
cards.answer: Four principles (Beauchamp & Childress): autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice — applied through best-interests assessment under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, involving family, IMCA if no representative, and shared decision-making.

cards.question: What is the distinction between withholding and withdrawing treatment?
cards.answer: Ethically and legally equivalent in UK law — both are decisions not to provide treatment that is not in the patient's best interests; withdrawal is not euthanasia, as intent is to relieve suffering, not to cause death (GMC 2010, Aintree v James 2013).

cards.question: How are prognostic scores used responsibly at end of life?
cards.answer: APACHE IV, SOFA and clinical frailty scales inform but never determine individual decisions; integrate with disease trajectory, response to treatment and patient values — never withdraw on score alone.
